text: Vavá's father is close to broke, and the son's answer is not to look for work but to look for a camera. The plan he brings to his friend Jandir is small and vicious: photograph an uncle's lover, Leda, in a way the uncle would pay to keep private, then name the price. Ruy Guerra shot this in 1962 at a hundred minutes, with the loose, unhurried rhythm of people who have never had to be anywhere on time. The crime is almost beside the point; the pressure is class. These are boys with the manners of money and none of the money, and the blackmail is an attempt to stay in a life whose bill has arrived. What lingers is how easily the scheme turns a woman into an instrument, and how long the film lets that ease stand in frame without comment.

A middle-class man exchanges a few words with a stranger at an airport, and that is the whole of his crime. Jofre Godoi da Fonseca has no politics to speak of; what he has is a comfortable distance from other people's trouble. The political police take him for Sarmento, an opposition figure he happened to stand next to, and the arrest proceeds from a file rather than from anything he has done. Roberto Farias set the story in the mid-1970s, when the economic miracle and the World Cup gave the dictatorship a great deal of noise to work behind, and filmed it in 1982, close enough that both were still household memory. The first stretch stays in the unremarkable middle-class life of a man with no reason to expect trouble, and the film is patient about how little has to go wrong before he is required to prove what he is not.

The town is in Minas Gerais, small enough that a new priest counts as an event and a young woman's afternoon counts as public information. Joaquim Pedro de Andrade takes ninety minutes to work out what that arrangement costs. The priest holds his standing by being the one man exempt from wanting anything; the moment he wants something, that exemption is the currency he is spending. She has less room still, since whatever she does will be read for her by people who had settled their opinion before she arrived at one of her own. The attraction is treated less as a secret than as a slow public fact, gathering in doorways and at the edge of Mass. Much of the tension comes from how many people see it long before anyone will say it aloud.

Sixty-four minutes, two stories, and no visible effort to reconcile them. One belongs to a man in a low middle-class Rio apartment who kills his parents with a razor and then does what the title says. The other belongs to Marcia, rich and dissatisfied, who uses her husband's absence to go up to Petrópolis, where an old friend, Regina, comes to visit. Júlio Bressane made this in 1969 and leaves the seam between the halves open; the effect is less mystery than adjacency, a country in which the same afternoon holds both. Flatness is the method. The violence is delivered with the intonation of an errand, and the leisure in Petrópolis is filmed with exactly as much heat, which is to say that the comedy — and there is comedy — comes from a camera that declines to grade what it looks at.

Graciliano Ramos wrote novels and held public office, and in the 1930s an accusation of communist sympathy was enough to end the usefulness of both. He was sent to Ilha Grande and held among the common prisoners, and Nelson Pereira dos Santos gives that fact one hundred and ninety minutes. The length is the argument. A short film about imprisonment can register the shock of it; at this scale the subject becomes duration — what a day costs when there are hundreds of them, and what a writer's standing is worth in a place with no use for it. Brazil sent it to the Academy Awards as its international entry. What stays is the company rather than the charge: the men around Ramos were not accused of politics at all, and the film keeps him among them rather than above them.

Nhô Quim wants red meat, and not as one wish among others: it is the only thing he has ever asked of his life. Carula wants a husband, and her father owns an ox he will kill for the wedding, so two hungers can be settled in a single afternoon — provided Nhô Quim passes the tests set to prove he is worth the animal. André Klotzel keeps it to seventy-seven minutes, the right length for a joke that runs on courtship ritual and does not pretend to be about anything grander than what people will agree to in order to eat. The comedy is dry. Nhô Quim is not a fool; he is a man from a place where beef is an occasion. The scarcity underneath the joke is never disguised, and the film declines to be solemn about a man whose whole ambition is dinner.

A songwriter in the northern zone of Rio makes sambas good enough to travel further than he ever will. Nelson Pereira dos Santos spends eighty-three minutes on the distance between making something and being paid for it. The music is not atmosphere here; it is the product, and the film keeps returning to the fact that a song leaves the room more easily than the person who wrote it. Injustice, in this account, is not an incident that can be resolved before the last reel. It is the arrangement the songwriter has to keep working inside, which is harder to dramatise and harder to end. What results is closer to a portrait than a plot: a talent examined at the exact point where talent stops being enough, in a city with settled ideas about which of its neighbourhoods make things and which are paid for them.

A movie camera in 1930s Brazil is rare enough that pointing one at a wanted man becomes a transaction rather than an ambush. The photographer is Lebanese and lives in Brazil; the wanted man is Lampião, and the footage he manages to shoot is the whole subject. Made in 1997, more than sixty years after the fact, the film is at least as interested in the act of recording as in the outlaws recorded — what it takes to get near them, what the images are worth afterward, and who wants a picture of himself in circulation. Ninety-three minutes, and the bandits know the camera is there. That knowledge sits under every encounter: men with reputations to keep, meeting a stranger who owns the means of keeping them, neither party naive about the exchange.

The road is the Trans-Amazon, and the film travels it in the cab of a truck hauling timber. Iracema came to Belém from the countryside for the Círio de Nazaré and never went home; by the time she talks her way into the ride, the dance clubs have already made their claim on her. Jorge Bodanzky keeps the fiction thin enough to see through. The fires at the roadside, the men working under conditions nobody would call employment, the girls younger than she is — none of it is set dressing; it is the country the truck is driving past in 1975. Brazilian censors kept the film out of cinemas for years. Ninety-six minutes, two people in a cab, and a conversation that keeps circling what each thinks the other is worth: she wants the Southeast, and he has the wheel.

A girl is raised to know nothing, and then left in a room with a man who knows exactly what he wants. Her mother's piety is not consolation but government; her father runs the household as a jurisdiction. Seventy-six minutes, and the result is a study of ignorance as something done to a person rather than a state she happens to be in: she cannot name what is happening, because naming it was never permitted. Leopoldo Torre Nilsson stays inside the house, where the ordinary furniture of respectability does most of the coercion. The man is her father's friend, so the family's own code of hospitality is what delivers her to him. Argentina, 1957. The film is far more exact about the machinery of that arrangement than about anyone's feelings, and the exactness is what makes it cold to sit with.

A fortune teller tells Zulmira that a blonde woman will disturb her peace, and she leaves with the prophecy already hunting for a face. Her husband, Toninho, is consulted. Her cousin Glorinha is blonde. Out of that small piece of arithmetic Leon Hirszman builds ninety-six minutes on how a superstition, once accepted, reorganises a marriage around itself — who is looked at, what a silence is taken to mean, which ordinary courtesy now reads as proof. Zulmira is not stupid. She is a woman with very little authority over her circumstances who has been handed one explanation that fits everything, and the film understands how much sense there is in keeping it. Nothing dramatic has to happen for a household to become unlivable; the suspicion does the work, and it is patient.

Two brothers report a man missing, and the police arrest the brothers. The film establishes early that they did not do it, then spends ninety-two minutes on the machinery that produces a confession anyway. Luiz Sérgio Person reconstructs the procedure step by step: torture, applied methodically, extended to the wives, and converted into a signed document that everyone downstream is free to treat as truth. The interest is administrative as much as moral. A false confession has to be written, witnessed and filed by men with every professional reason to believe it, and the film follows each of those movements with an accountant's patience. Brazil put it forward for the international Academy Award. Its worst passages are conducted in the tone of routine work, which is the part that stays.

Paulo has a working method with women, and it survives everything until he meets a friend's fiancée. He decides she is all women at once, which sounds like devotion and is closer to bookkeeping: it lets him keep every appetite while announcing that he has given them up. Domingos de Oliveira plays it light — conversation, apartments, people with enough leisure to discuss their own desires at length — and gives Paulo ninety minutes to sit with a choice he has already been handed. The pleasure is in watching him avoid it. The joke underneath, and it is a real joke, is that the flattery he offers her cannot be told apart from the habit he claims to be breaking. Whether he has ever looked at a person rather than a category is the thing the comedy keeps circling, and it is funnier about the failure than it is forgiving.

A man kills his wife on their wedding night, is acquitted, and moves to the country. The court has finished with him; the film has not. Humberto Mauro gives the rest of seventy-eight minutes to what happens when such a person is absorbed into an ordinary place — work, neighbours, and in time a woman with another man's claim on her. The 1933 date shows in the method: faces and gesture carry the weight, and desire registers physically, without the explanatory vocabulary a later film would reach for. Nothing in the setup asks for sympathy, and none is offered. What holds the attention is the refusal to punish or absolve; the camera keeps watching a man whose violence a court has already excused, and leaves the countryside to make its own arrangement with him.
